# Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment

Guoqing Zhang    Rafik Hadfi    Takayuki Ito

###### Abstract

Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission following
hospital discharge is a major benchmark for evaluating healthcare
quality and patient safety in modern critical care medicine. Most
existing predictive approaches assume that readmission risk is
determined solely by a patient’s individual pathophysiological state,
ignoring the institution’s resource capacity and operational context
(Hospital Operational Context). In clinical practice, discharge
decisions are frequently dynamic trade-offs made by intensivists
balancing patient medical stability against ward bed turnover pressures.
To address this gap, we design an Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical
Decision Support System (CDSS) for ICU discharge risk assessment. On the
one hand, the system unites multi-agent collaborative extraction with
self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate
formatting-template noise across lengthy progress notes. On the other
hand, it constructs departmental workload indicators (icu_speedup_los)
alongside admission flow characteristics, unifying continuous vital
signs, hierarchical sparse medical codes (ICD/DRG), and discharge
summary semantics. Addressing the extreme class imbalance ($`\sim`$10.5%
readmission incidence) and the challenge of alarm fatigue, the system
implements data normalization, class reweighting optimization, and an F1
decision-threshold calibration pipeline. In 20 independent multi-seed
runs conducted on a cohort of 20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical
findings show that: a single-modality baseline depending exclusively on
vital signs possesses limited predictive capacity under real-world class
imbalance (PR-AUC of only $`0.1387\pm 0.0086`$); directly concatenating
raw text embeddings causes performance degradation in decision tree
models (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030,
respectively); whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture
(Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter freezing and
differential learning rates successfully reverses text negative
transfer, achieving the overall highest AUROC of $`0.8288\pm 0.0110`$,
PR-AUC of $`0.4373\pm 0.0310`$, and a competitive F1-Score of
$`0.4757\pm 0.0196`$. Mechanistic attribution analyses also confirm that
operational indicators supply independent risk signals, establishing an
engineering foundation for deploying high-utility clinical decision
support tools in bedside hospital wards.

Code — https://github.com/KuoChing-cmd/ClinicalNoteAgent/

## S1 Introduction

In intensive care clinical decision-making, identifying vulnerable
patients at risk of latent deterioration and avoiding premature
step-down to general wards are core imperatives of critical care
medicine. Patients experiencing unplanned ICU readmission within 30 days
of discharge undergo substantially prolonged hospital stays and face
elevated in-hospital mortality ([Klinge et al. 2020](#bib.bib13);
[Barbieri et al. 2020](#bib.bib2); [Sheetrit, Brief, and Elisha
2023](#bib.bib19)). While recent multicenter investigations confirm the
promise of machine learning for post-discharge surveillance ([Lim et al.
2025](#bib.bib15)), existing clinical early warning systems commonly
encounter barriers during ward deployment due to alarm fatigue: in
low-prevalence locales where readmissions occur in only $`\sim`$10% of
cases, typical models optimized for high AUROC tend to trigger
substantial false-positive alarms, prompting clinicians to turn off the
alert systems. To construct an actionable Clinical Decision Support
System (CDSS), one must preserve screening sensitivity while
substantially improving precision, thereby driving PR-AUC and F1 scores
toward clinically acceptable operating points.

Although electronic health record (EHR) repositories such as MIMIC-III
([Johnson et al. 2016](#bib.bib9)) have advanced machine learning in
critical care—spanning deep temporal focus ([Madinei, Keyvanpour, and
Shojaedini 2024](#bib.bib18)), graphical EHR representations ([Choi
et al. 2020](#bib.bib5)), and recent readmission benchmarks ([Fathy,
Emeriaud, and Cheriet 2025](#bib.bib7))—state-of-the-art predictive
models still encounter two fundamental deployment bottlenecks. First,
they exhibit a neglect of hospital operational context. Standard models
conceptualize patients as closed physiological entities, presuming that
deterioration following transfer stems entirely from built-in disease
progression. In clinical practice, however, ICU discharge is
fundamentally a resource deployment and scheduling process carried out
under institutional bed constraints ([Kim et al. 2015](#bib.bib11);
[Wagner et al. 2013](#bib.bib22); [Long and Mathews 2018](#bib.bib16)).
Intensivists must routinely weigh incomplete physiological recovery
against acute bed demands driven by emergency department (ED) boarding
or post-operative transfers. Patient transfer frequency before ICU
admission, ED boarding durations, and ward acceleration driven by bed
saturation directly mirror operational workflow strain and care
coordination friction; yet, customary doctrines remain entirely agnostic
to this systemic background. Second, models suffer from data disparity
and text template noise. Intensive care records span high-frequency
temporal streams, sparse diagnostic codes, and lengthy unstructured
progress notes. While recent studies explore medical text via knowledge
graphs ([Lu, Nguyen, and Dou 2021](#bib.bib17)) or multimodal
architectures for readmission prediction ([Helmy et al.
2025](#bib.bib8); [Datta et al. 2025](#bib.bib6)), clinical free-text is
often lengthy, laden with jargon, and burdened by copy-pasted
administrative templates. Directly feeding unadapted high-dimensional
text embeddings fails to yield meaningful gains and instead introduces
severe feature interference (negative transfer) with strong baselines
such as gradient-boosted decision trees.

To resolve these problems, we reframe ICU discharge evaluation as an
operationally aware multimodal decision-support task and develop a CDSS
architecture that encompasses self-evolving textual distillation and
deep cross-modal correlation. The core contributions of this paper are
summarized as follows:

- •
  Operation-aware Decision Framework: Overcoming randomized timestamp
  offsets in MIMIC-III, we introduce unit-benchmarked turnover deviation
  indicators (icu_speedup_los) and care flow complexity features,
  eliminating the subjective assumption that outcomes depend solely on
  physiological status.
- •
  Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Text Distillation: We formulate a 7-domain
  specialist agent collaborative division of labor paired with a
  reflective evolutionary experience repository, accumulating 3,085
  rules across 5,000 patient samples. Combined with FAISS vector
  retrieval for structured information distillation, we propose a
  layer-wise, frozen, end-to-end fine-tuning scheme that systematically
  mitigates interference from template noise in clinical notes.
- •
  Thorough Testing under Low-Prevalence Conditions: Across a cohort of
  20,000 ICU stays, we conduct 20 independent randomized multi-seed runs
  (Seeds 42–61), exposing the weakness of single-modality physiological
  prediction (PR-AUC of only 0.1387) and verifying the robustness of the
  end-to-end fine-tuning architecture in achieving global optimality
  (AUROC 0.8288, PR-AUC 0.4373, F1 0.4757).
- •
  Interpretability & Clinical Utility Analysis: Through integrated
  gradients ([Sundararajan, Taly, and Yan 2017](#bib.bib20)), we
  systematically explain the mechanistic contributions of separate
  physiological channels, pivotal time-based attention windows, and
  operational flow variables in 30-day readmission forecasting.

## S2 Clinical Workflow and Problem Formulation

### S2.1 Clinical Prediction Task and Endpoint Definition

The prediction target is unplanned ICU readmission within 30 days
following discharge (30-Day Readmission). In light of complex
intra-hospital patient trajectories, endpoint labels $`y_{i}\in\{0,1\}`$
follow strict clinical mutually exclusive criteria:

- •
  Cross-admission readmission: The patient undergoes a separate hospital
  admission and enters an ICU within 30 days post-discharge (same
  SUBJECT_ID, distinct HADM_ID).
- •
  Within-admission readmission: During the same hospitalization episode,
  the patient is transferred out of the ICU, deteriorates, and is
  subsequently readmitted back to the ICU (multiple ICU stays under the
  same HADM*ID, where the subsequent admission timestamp postdates the
  preceding transfer timestamp, i.e.,
  $`\text{INTIME}*{k+1}>\text{OUTTIME}\_{k}`$).
- •
  Mortality Mutual-Exclusion: Patients who suffer in-hospital mortality
  (HOSPITAL_EXPIRE_FLAG = 1) have their readmission risk strictly
  calibrated to 0, eliminating logical contradictions.

### S2.2 Multimodal Clinical Data Streams and Domain Alignment

For each ICU stay event $`i\in\{1,\dots,N\}`$ (experimental cohort
$`N=20,000`$), the input is structured as a heterogeneous quadruple:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{X}_{i}=\left\{\mathbf{X}_{i}^{seq},\mathbf{x}_{i}^{stat},\mathbf{x}_{i}^{code},\mathbf{x}_{i}^{text}\right\}
``` |  | (S1) |

First, for high-frequency dynamic physiological sequences
($`\mathbf{X}_{i}^{seq}\in\mathbb{R}^{48\times 8}`$), the system
captures 8 core physiological signs during the initial 48 hours
following ICU admission: Heart Rate (HR), Respiratory Rate (RR), Oxygen
Saturation ($`\text{SpO}_{2}`$), Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP),
Diastolic Blood Pressure (DBP), Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP),
Temperature (Temp), and Blood Glucose (Glucose). Blood pressure
measurements explicitly distinguish invasive arterial pressure from
non-invasive cuff pressure; when both coexist, the invasive arterial
line—the gold standard in critical care—is preferred. Time series are
resampled into 1-hour regularized bins, with missing steps
forward-filled.

Second, structured demographic and operational indicators
($`\mathbf{x}_{i}^{stat}\in\mathbb{R}^{15}`$) capture baseline patient
context and care delivery friction across three facets: (i) Baseline &
Surgical covariates include age, gender, marital status, ethnicity,
insurance, admission source/type, first ICU unit, surgical procedure
count, surgery binary indicator, and log-transformed surgery-to-ICU
entry gap $`\ln(1+\Delta t_{\text{surg}})`$. (ii) Transfer Patterns
track the number of ward transfers prior to ICU admission
(pre_icu_transfers) along with log-transformed emergency department wait
time $`\ln(1+t_{\text{ED}})`$. (iii) Ward Pressure & Turnover Deviation:
addressing the obstacle where randomized absolute timestamps in
MIMIC-III preclude concurrent bed occupancy observation across patients,
we formulate a stay deviation metric aligned with historical unit
benchmarks (e.g., MICU, SICU) along with stay duration features:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{icu\_speedup\_los}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\overline{\text{LOS}}_{\text{unit}}-\text{LOS}_{\text{actual}}`$ |  | (S2) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{log\_icu\_los}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\ln(1+\text{LOS}_{\text{hours}})`$ |  |  |

Specifically, under a zero-leakage cutoff, the feature is strictly
computed at the exact moment of the step-down transfer order, sharing
the same temporal cross-section with discharge notes and precluding
future information leakage. Crucially, contrary to the naive assumption
that shorter stays merely reflect milder acuity (which would yield lower
readmission rates), empirical attribution reveals that positive
icu_speedup_los (early turnover) significantly correlates with higher
readmission risk (20.1% continuous IG attribution). This refutes
indication confounding and confirms that the metric captures external
operational bed-turnover pressure and premature discharge before
complete physiological stabilization.

Third, hierarchically decoupled sparse medical codes
($`\mathbf{x}_{i}^{code}`$) capture hierarchical EHR coding structures
([Choi et al. 2020](#bib.bib5)). Primary ICD diagnoses and primary DRG
codes select the Top-128 categories, mapped into categorical indices
feeding a learnable continuous embedding layer (128 dimensions).
Secondary diagnoses (Top-32), surgical procedures (Top-64), and
prescribed medications (Top-64) are encoded into multi-hot sparse
vectors, projected through embedding weight matrices, mean-pooled across
active entries, and concatenated into compact representations.

Fourth, unformatted clinical progress representations
($`\mathbf{x}_{i}^{text}`$) incorporate free-text clinical progress
notes. In contrast to standard clinical text baselines ([Lu, Nguyen, and
Dou 2021](#bib.bib17); [Helmy et al. 2025](#bib.bib8)) that directly
process progress notes vulnerable to template noise, lengthy inpatient
records are distilled via self-evolving multi-agent workflows into
structured summaries, with 768-dimensional semantic features extracted
by Bio_ClinicalBERT ([Alsentzer et al. 2019](#bib.bib1)).

## S3 Operation-aware CDSS Architecture

Figure S1: System overview of the Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical
Decision Support System (CDSS). (a) Multimodal EHR inputs aligned with
hospital operational bottleneck perception; (b) Self-evolving
multi-agent clinical RAG mining pipeline with 7 domain specialists and
dual-track rule/case repositories; (c) Parallel feature derivation and
Late Fusion architecture alongside the Bio_ClinicalBERT end-to-end
fine-tuning pathway; (d) Zero-leakage normalization, alarm-fatigue
calibrated thresholds, and bedside risk-stratified decision support.

### S3.1 Unstructured Text Mining: Multi-Agent Self-Evolving RAG Mechanism

Orchestrated multi-agent architectures sustain diagnostic fidelity under
complex clinical workloads compared to monolithic models ([Klang et al.
2026](#bib.bib12)). To overcome verbosity and repetitive administrative
boilerplate in clinical progress notes, the system establishes a
self-evolving multi-agent distillation pipeline across five coordinated
stages: (i) Hierarchical Specialist Collaboration: Clinical text is
segmented across 7 specialized clinical domains (Nursing, Radiology, ICU
Care, ECG, Attending Physician, Discharge Summary, and
Echocardiography), where independent domain agents extract acute warning
signals. (ii) Meta-Agent Synthesis: A supervisory Meta-Agent aggregates
domain summaries, synthesizing a structured JSON report containing a
prioritized vital factor roster and composite risk score.
(iii) Reflective Evolution Loop: When predictions diverge from clinical
ground truth during training, a Reflection Agent audits causal failure
points, extracting physician-vetted heuristic rules into a knowledge
base (3,085 rules); correctly classified trajectories are cataloged as
gold-standard exemplars (1,899 cases). (iv) Lightweight RAG Retrieval:
Guided by all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings and a FAISS index, the pipeline
dynamically retrieves the Top-5 relevant heuristic rules and Top-1
exemplar case per admission as few-shot in-context demonstrations.
(v) Feature Embedding & Projection: Distilled summaries are encoded by
Bio_ClinicalBERT into 768-dimensional contextual vectors and projected
to a $`d`$-dimensional embedding $`\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{note}}`$ aligned
with temporal representations.

### S3.2 Cross-Modal Network Architecture and Deep Fusion Schemes

The framework investigates three architectural paradigms. First, we
evaluate tree-based baselines: XGBoost ([Chen and Guestrin
2016](#bib.bib4)) and LightGBM ([Ke et al. 2017](#bib.bib10)) fitted on
physically concatenated vectors combining temporal statistical
aggregations, static covariates, multi-hot codes, and 768-dimensional
text embeddings ([Chen et al. 2025](#bib.bib3)). Second, we construct
sequential late fusion (LSTM Late Fusion): a 4-layer bi-directional LSTM
with self-attentive temporal pooling encodes physiological sequences,
concatenated at the classification tier with static, code, and text
representations projected via independent MLP branches. Third, we
formulate parallel multi-branch extraction and late fusion. Dynamic
physiological sequences are encoded via a deep Transformer encoder
([Vaswani et al. 2017](#bib.bib21)) into $`\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{cls}}`$;
static operational indicators and medical codes are mapped via
independent MLPs into dense vectors $`\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{ops}}`$ and
$`\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{code}}`$. These representations are concatenated
with text embedding $`\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{note}}`$ to form
$`\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{fused}}=[\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{cls}}\parallel\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{ops}}\parallel\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{code}}\parallel\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{note}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{2d+64}`$,
feeding a 2-layer MLP head for joint risk estimation. To prevent
representational collapse during end-to-end training, the initial 8
layers of Bio_ClinicalBERT are frozen, leaving deeper layers (Layers
9–12) active; BERT parameters receive a 0.1$`\times`$ scaled learning
rate (lr \* 0.1) with gradient checkpointing enabled.

### S3.3 Training Optimization and Leak-Free Validation Protocols

To ensure leak-free evaluation under severe class imbalance
($`\sim`$10.5% prevalence) and achieve stable multimodal convergence, we
institute four disciplined methodological safeguards: (i) Zero-Leakage
Normalization: StandardScaler parameters are fitted strictly on training
splits; validation and testing cohorts inherit these statistics without
re-estimation, precluding distribution leakage. (ii) Dynamic
Cost-Sensitive Loss: To counter minority-class sparsity, a weighted
binary cross-entropy loss deploys dynamic inverse class ratio weighting
derived strictly from the training split:
$`w_{\mathrm{pos}}=N_{\mathrm{neg}}/N_{\mathrm{pos}}\approx 8.97`$.
(iii) Cosine Scheduling & Rollback: A CosineAnnealingLR schedule
regulates learning rate decay, paired with early stopping (patience=15)
on validation loss; upon termination, model parameters rollback to the
checkpoint achieving the minimal validation loss. (iv) Decision
Threshold Calibration: On validation splits, exhaustive grid search
(step size 0.01) determines the optimal decision cutoff $`t^{*}`$
maximizing the $`F_{1}`$-Score, replacing the uncalibrated default 0.5
threshold for final test evaluation.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Model Category | Model Name & Variant | Optimal Threshold $`t^{*}`$ | AUROC | PR-AUC | F1-Score |
| Tree Baselines & Text Ablation | XGBoost Base | $`0.314\pm 0.093`$ | $`0.8055\pm 0.0098`$ | $`0.4125\pm 0.0209`$ | $`0.4465\pm 0.0193`$ |
|  | XGBoost + LLM Notes | $`0.134\pm 0.053`$ | $`0.7914\pm 0.0118`$ | $`0.3893\pm 0.0213`$ | $`0.4400\pm 0.0166`$ |

| Deep Multimodal Networks & Fusion | LSTM Base (Pure Structured) | $`0.747\pm 0.051`$ | $`0.8251\pm 0.0117`$ | $`0.4360\pm 0.0305`$ | $`\mathbf{0.4798\pm 0.0200}`$ |
|  | LSTM LateFusion (+ Notes) | $`0.726\pm 0.034`$ | $`0.8258\pm 0.0091`$ | $`0.4338\pm 0.0301`$ | $`0.4791\pm 0.0193`$ |

## S4 Experimental Evaluation and Validation

### S4.1 Evaluation Protocol and Cohort Setup

Experiments are run across 20,000 ICU stay records from the MIMIC-III
database. The cohort is partitioned into training (14,000 stays),
validation (2,000 stays), and test splits (4,000 stays) in a 7:1:2
ratio, with positive readmission prevalence ranging from 10.5% to 11.4%.
To eliminate partitioning anomalies, all candidate approaches are
evaluated across 20 independent randomized runs (Seeds 42–61), with test
performance reported as $`\text{Mean}\pm\text{Std}`$.

### S4.2 Comprehensive Performance Comparison and Paradigm Defense

Table [S1](#S3.T1 "Table S1 ‣ S3.3 Training Optimization and Leak-Free Validation Protocols ‣ S3 Operation-aware CDSS Architecture ‣ Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment")
summarizes the evaluation measures across 15 model configurations
evaluated at their optimal F1 decision thresholds across 20 randomized
runs. Three core empirical insights emerge. First, we observe text
negative transfer in shallow concatenation. Directly appending unadapted
768-d text embeddings into decision trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) triggers
notable performance decline. Inpatient notes are saturated with
administrative templates and boilerplate shorthand; high-dimensional
embeddings diffuse greedy tree node splitting, diluting compact,
high-SNR physiological and operational signals. Second, results
demonstrate the strength of structured baselines and multimodal
reframing. Purely structured LSTM Base establishes a solid benchmark
($`F_{1}=0.4798`$), demonstrating the fitting efficiency of recurrent
cells over 48-hour dynamics along with discrete codes. The multimodal
goal is therefore not to surpass structured models trivially, but to
resolve a harder clinical challenge: safely incorporating high-value
text semantics without suffering negative transfer (as observed in
Transformer EarlyFusion, which degrades under raw text noise). Third, we
achieve a reversal of negative transfer via end-to-end fine-tuning. With
layer-wise parameter freezing (Layers 9–12 active) and differential
learning rates, Transformer E2E FineTune is the sole architecture
reversing text negative transfer into positive gains, securing global
peaks in both AUROC ($`0.8288`$) and PR-AUC ($`0.4373`$). Paired
hypothesis tests across 20 matched random seeds confirm that the AUROC
gain of end-to-end fine-tuning over static early fusion is highly
statistically significant (mean AUROC 0.8288 vs. 0.8177; Paired
$`t`$-test $`t=4.89,p<0.001`$; Wilcoxon $`p<0.001`$). This provides
strong empirical evidence that end-to-end backpropagation prevents the
text representation from being overshadowed by dense temporal dynamics,
enabling the language model to better align textual risk cues with
structured physiological trajectories.

### S4.3 Sensor Dropout Robustness

In operational ICU environments, electrode detachment, patient movement,
and intermittent contact failures occur frequently. To assess fault
tolerance under incomplete physiological telemetry, we evaluated the
representative LSTM LateFusion model under random telemetry loss (Sensor
Dropout from 10% to 30%) across 20 independent runs. The system
presented remarkable stability: under 30% channel dropout, AUROC decayed
by less than 0.0005 in absolute terms (from $`0.8258\pm 0.0091`$ to
$`0.8254\pm 0.0092`$), PR-AUC remained steady ($`0.4338\to 0.4330`$),
and $`F_{1}`$ was preserved at $`0.4783\pm 0.0189`$. This confirms that
multimodal fusion provides robust cross-modal safety redundancy, in
which static operational indicators, diagnostic codes, and clinical text
insulate decision support due to localized telemetry disruptions.

### S4.4 Modal Ablation and Vitals Collapse

Feature ablation displays strong asymmetries across modalities. Relying
exclusively on 48-hour vital signs (LSTM Base (Only Vitals))
precipitates catastrophic collapse: AUROC plummets to $`0.6232`$ and
PR-AUC crashes to $`0.1387`$ (only marginally above the $`\sim`$10.5%
prevalence baseline), yielding an $`F_{1}`$ of only $`0.2213`$. This
demonstrates the inherent insufficiency of unimodal physiological
surveillance: immediate vitals capture transient acute acuity, whereas
chronic comorbidities and systemic operational friction primarily govern
30-day outcomes. Conversely, static demographics and coding alone (Only
Static & Codes) sustain an AUROC of $`0.8227`$ and PR-AUC of $`0.4294`$
($`|\Delta\text{prob}|=0.1437`$), establishing patient baseline and
operational pressures as basic priors, with dynamic vitals
($`|\Delta\text{prob}|=0.1014`$) providing acute trajectory corrections.

## S5 Mechanistic Attribution and Case Study

Figure S2: Feature attribution and ablation analysis of multimodal model
results. (a) Integrated Gradients (IG) importance across temporal
physiological channels; (b) Ablation contribution magnitude across core
input modalities ($`|\Delta\text{prob}|`$); (c) Temporal self-attention
weight distribution over the 48-hour sequence; (d) Top-10 ranked static
operational and demographic features by ablation importance.

### S5.1 Multimodal Attribution: Channels, Dynamics, and Operations

Integrated Gradients (IG) and attention analyses uncover collaborative
mechanisms throughout modalities
(Figure [S2](#S5.F2 "Figure S2 ‣ S5 Mechanistic Attribution and Case Study ‣ Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment")).
First, regarding vital sign dynamics, Heart Rate (32.0%) and Temperature
(22.2%) account for over half of physiological IG attribution,
reflecting cardiovascular reserve compensation and occult infection as
primary discharge stability determinants. Blood glucose (13.7%), SBP
(12.5%), and $`\text{SpO}_{2}`$ (10.3%) supply secondary warnings
against unmitigated glycemic swings and tissue hypoperfusion. Second,
with respect to time-based attention focus, attention concentrates
heavily on initial admission ($`t\in[0,2]`$ h, Hour 0 weight = 0.0806),
showing that initial resuscitation difficulty strongly anchors
downstream readmission risk. Across the 48h trajectory, intermediate
monitoring (12–36h, 42.3%) and acute admission (0–12h, 37.9%) dominate
reasoning, while pre-discharge attention declines (36–48h, 19.7%),
indicating that the model assesses stabilization effort rather than
superficial pre-discharge calm. Third, empirical findings establish the
primacy of operational friction. Pre-ICU transfer frequency
(pre_icu_transfers) accounts for 28.2% of static ablation and 50.9% of
continuous feature IG attribution, dominating all covariates. Ward
turnover pressure (icu_speedup_los) contributes 9.6% of ablation and
20.1% of continuous IG, proving that bed-saturation-driven premature
discharge elevates hidden deterioration risks, alongside surgical count
(surg_count) and gap.

### S5.2 Typical Clinical Case Vignette

A 68-year-old patient admitted with respiratory failure achieved stable
vitals after 48 hours in the ICU (normal BP and HR). Conventional
heuristics mirroring vitals-only logic would categorize the patient as
fully ready for discharge. However, our CDSS detected that before ICU
admission, the patient spent over 16 hours boarding in the emergency
department and underwent two intra-hospital transfers (pre_icu_transfers
elevated); furthermore, the patient’s unit was under extreme bed strain
(icu_speedup_los notably positive). Synthesizing multimodal evidence,
the CDSS triggered an elevated-risk alert for handoff friction and
metabolic instability, prompting the intensivist to extend observation
by 24 hours and recheck blood gases, successfully avoiding premature
discharge and subsequent readmission.

## S6 Conclusion

Synthesizing system development and 20 experimental runs, we highlight
four engineering lessons for actual clinical AI adoption. First, we
recognize the limits of vitals-only monitoring: the catastrophic failure
of Only Vitals ($`F_{1}=0.2213`$) proves that immediate telemetry
reflects transient acuity rather than medium-term prognosis, mandating
holistic cross-modal modeling. Second, mitigating text template noise is
critical; because inpatient records are heavily contaminated with
administrative boilerplate, layer-wise parameter freezing and
differential learning rates are required to avoid text negative
transfer. Third, operational context acts as an endogenous risk: pre-ICU
transfer friction and turnover pressure account for over 70% of
continuous static attribution, demonstrating that institutional strain
is an endogenous risk driver rather than exogenous noise. Fourth,
threshold calibration is indispensable against alarm fatigue: in
low-prevalence settings ($`\sim`$10%), default 0.5 thresholds collapse
precision; dynamic validation-set grid search for $`t^{*}`$ is mandatory
to avoid alert abandonment.

Two-Stage Deployment Roadmap: Real-world EHR systems are optimized for
legal archiving rather than machine learning, and critical care cannot
tolerate trial-and-error on live patients. We propose a two-stage
deployment pathway: “Near-Term Silent Shadow Verification, Long-Term
Clinical Digital Twins.” In the near term, the CDSS interfaces
non-intrusively with EHR discharge order streams in Silent Shadow Mode
to quantify the utility of human-artificial intelligence collaboration.
In the long term, longitudinal EHR repositories enable high-fidelity
Clinical Digital Twins simulation sandboxes ([Li et al.
2024](#bib.bib14)), allowing multi-agent architectures to undergo safety
stress-testing in a parallel digital ward before deploying
high-assurance decision policies at the bedside.

## Appendix A Cohort Selection and Flow Diagram

### S1.1 Study Population and Cohort Derivation Protocol

This study derives its analytical cohort from the MIMIC-III v1.4
(Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III) database (Johnson et
al. 2016), which comprises comprehensive clinical records from all
intensive care admissions at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center
($`N=61,532`$ ICU stays across $`46,520`$ unique patients).

In contrast to conventional benchmark studies that apply post-hoc
demographic exclusions (e.g., arbitrarily dropping pediatric/neonatal
admissions or short stays), our study retains all real-world ICU care
units (including MICU, CSRU, CCU, SICU, TSICU, and NICU) to preserve
clinical generalizability. The end-to-end cohort derivation protocol is
illustrated in
Figure [S3](#A1.F3 "Figure S3 ‣ S1.1 Study Population and Cohort Derivation Protocol ‣ Appendix A Cohort Selection and Flow Diagram ‣ Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure S3: End-to-end cohort derivation flowchart detailing MIMIC-III
database linkage, endpoint indexing, cohort capacity cap, multimodal
feature alignment, and train/validation/test partitioning.

### S1.2 Clinical Endpoint (Ground Truth) Definition

The primary target outcome is 30-Day Unplanned ICU Readmission. In
critical care environments, patients frequently transfer between
emergency departments, surgical suites, and step-down units. A positive
binary ground truth label ($`Y=1`$) is rigorously assigned if either of
the following conditions holds:

1.  1.
    Cross-Admission Readmission (Condition A): The identical patient
    (indexed by ‘SUBJECT_ID‘) is discharged from the hospital and
    subsequently readmitted to an ICU under a distinct hospital
    admission (‘HADM_ID‘), where timestamps satisfy:

    |  |  |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|----|----|
    |  | $`\displaystyle\text{INTIME}_{\text{next}}`$ | $`\displaystyle>\text{OUTTIME}_{\text{current}}\quad\land`$ |  |  |
    |  | $`\displaystyle\text{INTIME}_{\text{next}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\text{OUTTIME}_{\text{current}}+30\,\text{days}`$ |  | (S3) |
2.  2.
    Within-Admission Bounce-Back (Condition B): Within the same hospital
    encounter (‘HADM_ID‘), the patient is transferred out of the ICU to
    a general or step-down ward, acutely deteriorates, and is readmitted
    to an ICU ($`\text{INTIME}>\text{OUTTIME}`$).

Competing Risk Censoring: In-hospital mortality represents a terminal
competing risk that precludes future post-discharge readmission.
Patients who expired during their hospital stay (HOSPITAL_EXPIRE_FLAG =
1) are censored with $`Y=0`$. In our final cohort of $`N=20,000`$ stays,
exactly $`2,000`$ patients ($`10.00\%`$) experienced 30-day readmission,
yielding a natural class imbalance ratio of $`1:9`$. During training,
this imbalance is calibrated via an inverse positive loss weight
$`w_{\text{pos}}=N_{\text{neg}}/N_{\text{pos}}\approx 8.97`$.

## Appendix C Multi-Agent Clinical Prompt Specifications

The distillation framework deploys a coordinated 3-tier hierarchical
agent structure built on Llama-3.1 (via Ollama local inference). The
prompt templates and system instructions for all three agent tiers are
given below.

### S3.1 Tier 1: Domain Specialist Extraction Agents

Each patient’s clinical note history is segmented into 7 clinical
categories: Nursing/other, Radiology, Nursing, ECG, Physician, Discharge
summary, and Echo. Each specialist evaluates up to 8,000 characters of
domain-specific narrative notes:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 --------------------------------------

2 DOMAIN EXPERT AGENT PROMPT TEMPLATE

3 --------------------------------------

4 You are an expert clinical AI. Analyze the following

5 {category} notes to extract critical information that

6 might predict 30-day hospital mortality or ICU readmission.

7 Focus on identifying any abnormal findings, unresolved

8 issues, or high-risk indicators specific to this domain.

9

10 {category} NOTES:

11 {notes_text}

12

13 Provide a concise, structured summary highlighting key

14 risk factors. Do not include introductory text.

15 --------------------------------------

Listing 1: Prompt template for Tier 1 Domain Specialist Agents.

### S3.2 Tier 2: Lead Clinical Supervisory Meta-Agent

The supervisory Meta-Agent aggregates the 7 distilled briefs. Through
FAISS RAG retrieval, it incorporates the Top-5 most semantically aligned
doctor rules and Top-1 golden exemplar trajectory, outputting a
calibrated JSON risk synthesis:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 --------------------------------------

2 LEAD CLINICAL META-AGENT PROMPT TEMPLATE

3 --------------------------------------

4 You are the lead meta-agent clinical AI. You will receive

5 summaries from various domain agents for a single patient’s

6 ICU stay.

7 Your task is to synthesize these summaries and produce a

8 final, structured JSON report identifying TWO distinct risks:

9 1. In-hospital mortality risk.

10 2. 30-day ICU readmission risk.

11

12 \### DOCTOR EXPERIENCE RULES TO FOLLOW:

13 {rules_text}

14

15 {few_shot_example}

16

17 \### PATIENT DOMAIN SUMMARIES:

18 {combined_category_summaries}

19

20 Output your analysis strictly in the following JSON format:

21 {

22 "mortality_risk_score": \<int 1-10, 10 highest\>,

23 "icu_readmission_risk_score": \<int 1-10, 10 highest\>,

24 "critical_factors_list": \["factor 1", "factor 2"\],

25 "final_summary": "\<A concise 2-3 sentence synthesis\>"

26 }

27 --------------------------------------

Listing 2: Prompt template for Tier 2 Lead Clinical Meta-Agent.

### S3.3 Tier 3: Clinical Reflection Agent

When Meta-Agent severity scores ($`\geq 7`$ vs. $`<7`$) contradict
ground-truth clinical endpoints during the evolutionary training phase,
the Reflection Agent audits diagnostic reasoning gaps and adds a new
heuristic rule to the repository:

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 --------------------------------------

2 CLINICAL REFLECTION AGENT PROMPT TEMPLATE

3 --------------------------------------

4 You are the Clinical Reflection Agent. The Meta-Agent just

5 made predictions about a patient’s mortality and ICU

6 readmission risk, but failed on one or both tasks.

7

8 ERRORS MADE:

9 {error_context}

10

11 Meta-Agent Output: {meta_summary_json}

12

13 Domain Summaries it based its decision on:

14 {category_summaries}

15

16 Analyze why the Meta-Agent failed specifically on the

17 mismatched task(s). Did it overweigh a symptom for

18 mortality? Did it ignore a resolved condition for

19 readmission?

20 Provide a single, concise RULE (1-2 sentences) starting

21 with either "\[Mortality Rule\]:" or "\[Readmission Rule\]:"

22 that should be added to the experience base.

23 DO NOT provide conversational text. Output ONLY the rule.

24 --------------------------------------

Listing 3: Prompt template for Tier 3 Clinical Reflection Agent.

## Appendix D Self-Evolving RAG Knowledge Bases

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Clinical Domain | Risk Task |  Rule Specification |
| Cardiovascular | Readmission |  \[Readmission Rule\]: In post-CABG or post-valve surgery patients, the emergence of new-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response represents an acute readmission hazard even if pharmacological or electrical cardioversion achieved transient sinus rhythm. |
| Cardiovascular | Mortality |  \[Mortality Rule\]: In acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock, persistent requirement for two or more concurrent vasoactive infusions (e.g., Norepinephrine $`+`$ Epinephrine) indicates extreme in-hospital mortality regardless of baseline LVEF. |
| Respiratory | Readmission |  \[Readmission Rule\]: If a patient was extubated within 24 hours prior to ICU discharge but presents residual tachypnea ($`\text{RR}>24`$) or requires escalating high-flow nasal cannula/BiPAP requirements, assign an elevated readmission risk. |
| Respiratory | Mortality |  \[Mortality Rule\]: If a patient treated for acute respiratory distress exhibits documented bilateral radiographic clearance and stable oxygenation on minimal supplemental oxygen ($`\text{FiO}_{2}<35\%`$), do not score high mortality risk solely based on initial intubation status. |
| Neurology | Mortality |  \[Mortality Rule\]: When physical examination satisfies brain death criteria or presents profound hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with absent brainstem reflexes, assign maximum mortality risk regardless of hemodynamic stability. |
| Neurology | Readmission |  \[Readmission Rule\]: Residual delirium, agitation, or confusion without acute focal neurological deficits increases nursing care friction but does not warrant elevated ICU readmission risk unless complicated by imminent airway compromise. |
| Infectious / Sepsis | Readmission |  \[Readmission Rule\]: Septic patients completing antibiotic therapy with normalized WBC/procalcitonin but persistent unexplained fever spikes must not be discharged without negative repeat blood cultures; elevate readmission risk. |
| Renal / Fluids | Readmission |  \[Readmission Rule\]: Acute kidney injury resolving with spontaneous diuresis can only be designated as low readmission risk if serum creatinine has stabilized or trended downward for at least 48 consecutive hours prior to transfer. |
| Discharge Flow | Readmission |  \[Readmission Rule\]: An elevated ICU readmission risk should be downgraded if pending laboratory abnormalities have been formally documented as clinically resolved and stable prior to signing final ward transfer orders. |
| Goals of Care | Readmission |  \[Readmission Rule\]: Do not predict elevated ICU readmission risk if remaining clinical complexity is driven by transitions to palliative comfort care, family DNR/DNI execution, or hospice placement rather than acute organ failure. |

Table S3: Representative physician-vetted heuristic experience rules
distilled by the Self-Evolving Reflection Agent.

### S4.1 Doctor Experience Rules Base (3,085 Rules)

Over the iterative training loop on $`14,000`$ training stays, the
reflection agent accumulated 3,085 rules:

- •
  Mortality Rules ($`N=2,951`$): Rules differentiating acute reversible
  organ decompensation from catastrophic multi-system failure.
- •
  Readmission Rules ($`N=2,773`$): Rules capturing premature discharge
  under ward saturation, incomplete diuretic titration, post-extubation
  subglottic stridor, and telemetry instability.

provides representative rules categorized across 7 core physiological

## Appendix E Hyperparameters and Experimental Setup

Table [S4](#A5.T4 "Table S4 ‣ Appendix E Hyperparameters and Experimental Setup ‣ Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment")
outlines all hyperparameter choices, optimization parameters, and model
specifications across architectures.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Component / Module | Hyperparameter Name | Value / Specification | Rationale / Design Justification |
| Cohort Splits | Total Cohort Size | $`20,000`$ aligned ICU stays | Filtered MIMIC-III adult stays with 48h data |
|  | Split Proportion | 70% Train / 10% Val / 20% Test | 14,000 / 2,000 / 4,000 sample partitioning |
|  | Randomization Seeds | 20 runs (Seeds 42–61) | Eliminates split-specific bias in evaluation |
|  | Loss Re-weighting | $`w_{\text{pos}}=8.97`$ | Dynamically matches negative-to-positive ratio in train split |
| Training Optimization | Maximum Epochs | $`200`$ epochs | Early stopping with patience $`=15`$ on validation loss |
|  | Mini-Batch Size | $`256`$ (End-to-End: $`64`$) | Balances throughput with gradient signal stability |
|  | Optimization Algorithm | AdamW (weight decay $`=10^{-4}`$) | Decoupled weight decay regularization |
|  | Base Learning Rate $`\eta`$ | $`5\times 10^{-4}`$ | Tuned for smooth multimodal cross-entropy convergence |
|  | Learning Rate Schedule | CosineAnnealingLR | Smooth decay to $`\eta_{\min}=5\times 10^{-6}`$ |
|  | Normalization Protocol | StandardScaler (Train-fit strictly) | Prevents temporal distribution leakage into validation/test |
| LSTM Architecture | Hidden State Dimension $`H`$ | $`128`$ ($`64`$ forward $`+`$ $`64`$ backward) | Sufficient capacity for 48h temporal abstractions |
|  | Recurrent Layer Depth | $`4`$ bidirectional layers | Deep feature extraction over physiological trajectories |
|  | Dropout Regularization | $`0.30`$ across recurrent states | Prevents co-adaptation of hidden states |
|  | Attention Pooling Dimension | $`128`$ | Normalized scalar projection of hidden states |
| Transformer Architecture | Latent Dimension $`d`$ | $`128`$ | Unified projection dimensionality across modalities |
|  | Multi-Head Attention Heads | $`4`$ heads (head dimension $`=32`$) | Multi-view temporal and tabular interaction |
|  | Transformer Layer Depth | $`2`$ encoder layers | Avoids over-parameterization on tabular EHR sequences |
|  | Feedforward Hidden Dimension | $`512`$ ($`4\times d`$) | Standard transformer non-linear expansion |
|  | Layer Normalization | Pre-LN (norm_first=True) | Stable gradient propagation without warmup sensitivity |
| Bio_ClinicalBERT E2E | Pretrained Backbone | emilyalsentzer/Bio_ClinicalBERT | 768-d domain prior pretrained on MIMIC notes |
|  | Maximum Token Length | $`512`$ WordPiece tokens | Maximum sequence capacity for clinical report summary |
|  | Differential LR Scaling | $`0.1\times`$ ($`\eta_{\text{BERT}}=5\times 10^{-5}`$) | Preserves pre-trained weights while adapting to readmission |
|  | Layer Freezing Strategy | Layers 1–8 Frozen; Layers 9–12 Active | Retains generic syntax; adapts deep semantic representations |
|  | Gradient Checkpointing | Enabled | Reduces activation memory footprint by 65% |
| Tree Baselines | Estimators / Maximum Depth | $`200`$ trees / Maximum depth $`6`$ | XGBoost and LightGBM configurations |
|  | Subsample / Colsample By Tree | $`0.80`$ row subsample / $`0.80`$ feature subsample | Tree-level feature and data bagging |
|  | Positive Class Balancing | scale_pos_weight = 8.97 | Aligns gradient tree splitting with binary loss reweighting |

### S7.2 Input Modality Leave-One-Out Ablation

Against the test cohort baseline predicted probability
($`\bar{p}=0.4041`$), leave-one-modality-out ablation yields: (1) Static
Covariates & Operations: $`|\Delta\text{prob}|=0.1437`$ (primary
baseline anchor); (2) 48h Longitudinal Vitals:
$`|\Delta\text{prob}|=0.1014`$ (acute physiological trajectory);
(3) Medical Codings (ICD/DRG/Rx): $`|\Delta\text{prob}|=0.0569`$
(comorbid chronic burden); and (4) Clinical Notes Embedding:
$`|\Delta\text{prob}|=0.0085`$ (residual semantic risk tuning).

### S7.3 Temporal Cross-Attention Dynamics

Transformer self-attention between the $`[\text{CLS}]`$ token and the 48
hourly vital sign vectors partitions into three clinically meaningful
phases: (1) Acute Resuscitation Phase (Hours 0–12): $`37.9\%`$ of total
attention, reflecting initial resuscitation response, drug loading, and
mechanical ventilation establishment; (2) Continuous Monitoring Phase
(Hours 12–36): $`42.3\%`$, capturing intermediate clinical stability and
multi-organ recovery; and (3) Pre-Discharge Tapering Phase (Hours
36–48): $`19.7\%`$, evaluating extubation tolerance, pressor weaning,
and ward readiness.
````
